references.text: God remembered Noah and all the wild animals and all the livestock that were with him in the ark. And God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters receded.
Abraham drew near and said: Will you then sweep away the righteous along with the wicked? ... So the Lord went his way after he had finished speaking with Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.
But when he hesitated, the men seized his hand and the hands of his wife and his two daughters, for the Lord's compassion was upon him. They brought him out and set him outside the city.

The whole land is sulfur and salt, a burnt-out wasteland. It is not sown, nothing sprouts there, and no grass grows there – a destruction like that of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which the Lord overthrew in his anger and wrath.

And he reduced the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes, condemning them to destruction, setting them as an example for those who would later live ungodly lives. But he rescued righteous Lot, who was distressed by the lawless conduct of the wicked.
Romans 4:3 gives the theological explanation for why God 'remembered Abraham' in Genesis 19:29, namely because of his faith that was credited to him as righteousness.
The rescue of Lot in Genesis 19:29 is a concrete example that God's promise to Abraham stands firm for his offspring, a principle Paul expands on theologically in Romans 4:16.
Proverbs 11:8 formulates the theological principle underlying the event in Genesis 19:29: the righteous (Lot) is saved while the wicked in the city are destroyed.
